report:
**Conclusion: no.** Current clinical evidence does not show that coenzyme Q10 (CoQ10) improves Parkinson’s movement symptoms or slows the motor/functional decline of Parkinson’s disease.

The strongest evidence is the Parkinson Study Group’s phase III randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial in early Parkinson’s. It tested high doses (1,200 or 2,400 mg/day) and was stopped early for futility: CoQ10 was generally safe and tolerated, but showed **no clinical benefit** versus placebo. This is particularly important because an earlier, smaller phase II trial had suggested a possible benefit; the larger confirmatory study did not reproduce it.  
https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/24664227/?dopt=Abstract

Evidence for a *symptomatic* motor benefit is also unconvincing. A multicenter randomized placebo-controlled trial specifically assessed symptomatic effects in people with Parkinson’s, rather than merely testing disease progression.  
https://jamanetwork.com/journals/jamaneurology/fullarticle/794066

A systematic review of CoQ10 across Parkinsonian syndromes similarly describes the clinical evidence as limited/inconsistent rather than demonstrating established benefit.  
https://www.mdpi.com/2075-4426/12/6/975

NIH’s National Center for Complementary and Integrative Health summarizes the practical bottom line: a major NIH-funded study found that even higher-than-usual CoQ10 doses did **not** improve symptoms in early Parkinson’s disease.  
https://www.nccih.nih.gov/health/coenzyme-q10

CoQ10 may be reasonable to discuss with a clinician for other individual reasons, but it should not replace proven Parkinson’s therapies, exercise/rehabilitation, or medication management.
